facts.fact: PD quotas account physical RAM. Init subdivides its budget; reference-account restrictions prevent arbitrary transfers across branches without parent mediation. Clients donate session quota before service creation and can request upgrades. Servers must undo session allocations before quota withdrawal; failures require parent policy, potentially destroying a sibling server or supplying more quota. Locally supplied or ancestor services retain authority over reclamation. Independent session backing stores are required: byte bookkeeping in a shared heap cannot ensure backing dataspaces can be freed. Resource requests may stall or trigger long operations; yield compliance is cooperative. Disk-space management belongs to servers, not the RAM quota contract.

sections: Ownership and lifetime of a session
facts.fact: Parents provide resources throughout child lifetime and control initial code, threads, capabilities and relationships. Children ultimately trust their parents. An established session directly connects client and server; intermediate policy components are outside its operation path. Session objects belong to the server and close follows the broker chain. A nonresponding server may block a client indefinitely. Parent destruction authority is not a numerical bound on complete teardown.

Core starts init and grants available resources, exposes physical resources through routed services, and provides bootstrap objects. PD sessions start with zero quota and have quota-bounded physical-memory and capability allocators. Closing a PD destroys its allocated dataspaces, removes their visibility across components and returns quota to the reference account. Dataspaces may be shared and mapped multiple times; contiguous RAM can serve as DMA buffers. Device, boot-ROM, CPU and mapping authority therefore belongs in the complete topology, not just guest RAM totals.

This historical release describes per-protection-domain kernel-memory accounting and quota exhaustion stopping a thread or invoking an OOM handler. The handler may transfer kernel quota, revoke delegations or stop the thread. Core's then-current IPC policy attempted an upgrade, then mapping revocation, then stopping; it was explicitly described as heuristic. This is evidence of the mechanism and policy distinction, not an immutable current NOVA configuration, fixed non-upgrading quota or complete current proof.

Genode's own VirtualBox 6 port was documented as an initial development snapshot running Linux and Windows guests, with limited multicore and preliminary integration. Kernel-agnostic virtualization interfaces replaced the NOVA-specific approach; readiness for other kernels was not universal tested feature parity. The same notes describe 64-bit AMD guests for VirtualBox 5. These are actual Genode-port claims, not merely upstream VirtualBox compatibility claims.

The newer official release announces Genode support for VirtualBox 7.2.14 after staff and community use, with newer Linux guests, improved multicore, UEFI, TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot including Windows 11. It states that the older VirtualBox 6.1 port had reached end of life. This narrows the guest-support feasibility gap but does not validate our exact guest image, CPython 3.12 x64 native artifacts, four installed forms or their resource and cleanup behavior.

Sculpt 25.10 documents an x86-64 system, VT-x for VirtualBox and recommended VT-d for driver sandboxing, plus Linux VM examples. Its service catalog includes virtualization, direct devices, storage, shared interfaces and powerful PD/tracing services. These require explicit routing and ownership decisions. This consulted Sculpt version is a documentation example, not a selected or asserted latest deployment; no boot, installation, guest or hardware setup was performed.

full_independent_primary_research.qualified_conclusion: The documented combination of physical RAM budgets, client-funded server allocations, kernel-resource quotas and Genode's actual Windows/Linux guest ports is a substantive whole-topology candidate. A quota parameter or guest-support statement alone is not positive admission. Exact selected configuration, donation and reclamation policies and every external backing owner still need one integrated allocation-and-authority graph.
missing_whole_domain_obligations: Freeze an exact supported kernel/core/init/VMM/driver build and source-to-binary provenance. Include static kernel, bootstrap, core, controller and allocator overhead, with fixed global and per-domain budgets and no unbudgeted automatic upgrades or transfers.

Prove per-session independent backing and all pending, retired, shared, mapped and cross-process ownership. Freeze failure policy for server close, blocked RPC, cooperative yield, insufficient quota and destruction; retain debt until actual release.

Provide continuous storage-byte and live-node enforcement separately, including disk images, metadata, deleted-open files, logs, brokers and backend caches. RAM donation is not a filesystem quota or cumulative-write bound.
Include DMA/IOMMU, device queues and passthrough, IPC and shared-folder/network crossings, external brokers and drivers in the authority and resource graph.
Establish exact Windows/Linux guest and interpreter/native dependency compatibility, complete resolver/host maps and source/wheel/sdist/repeat-build closure for the required four forms.

Provide supported bounded stop, cancel, drain, unmap, close, reap and physical reclamation across all owners, including failed startup. Neither cooperative policy nor logical session destruction supplies the complete numerical teardown bound.
